lessons.title: Calculate totals, payments and change
lessons.summary: Use unit prices and fixed charges to find a bill, check change and work with a simple budget.
lessons.objective: Use unit prices and fixed charges to find a bill, check change and work with a simple budget.
lessons.before: Write decimal prices clearly and check the unit beside each amount.
lessons.ideas:
Multiply each unit price by its quantity. Add the item costs and any fixed fee.

For change use the cash handed over minus the total cost. For a pot, begin with the opening amount, add receipts and subtract payments.

Set aside the fee. Divide what is left by the unit price. Use the greatest affordable whole number. Check the spending with that number.
lessons.method:
How do I build a total from a price list?

Write a line for each cost. For instance, a reader buying three £2.45 notebooks with one £1.80 collection fee writes an item subtotal and a single fee.

Which amounts are added and which are subtracted?

If the question asks what remains, check your answer against the amount available before you paid. It should be smaller unless money also came in.

How many whole items fit the budget?

A quotient of 6.8 means six whole items fit. Work out what six cost and subtract the complete bill from the original budget.
mistakes: A fixed charge is counted once. Multiplying the charge by the quantity makes the total too large.
Cash paid and goods bought are different amounts. Keep the cash payment separate from the bill until the subtraction for change.
Rounding up can buy an item that the budget cannot cover. Check that one more item would exceed the budget.

examples.solution:

Divide by the price per reel and take the whole number that fits. 7 reels cost £38.43.

Subtract that cost and the delivery charge from £42.02. This leaves £0.81.

lessons.title: Convert between currencies
lessons.summary: Read an exchange quote, choose the operation for each direction and compare prices in a common currency.
lessons.objective: Read an exchange quote, choose the operation for each direction and compare prices in a common currency.
lessons.before: Write decimal prices clearly and check the unit beside each amount.
lessons.ideas:
Starting from the quoted one-unit currency, multiply by the amount on the other side. For £1 = €1.23, multiply pounds by 1.23 to find euros.

From euros back to pounds, undo the previous multiplication. Divide the euro amount by the euros per pound.

For a fee deducted from the cash handed over, reduce that amount first. Then convert what remains.
lessons.method:
When do I multiply by the rate?

Test your operation on one pound first. It must produce €1.23. Then scale up to the amount in the question.

How do I go back the other way?

If £1 buys more than €1, the number of pounds will be smaller than the number of euros for the same amount of money. Check the size and write the requested precision.

How do I handle fees and compare prices?

When comparing prices, put both in the currency requested in the question. Subtract the lower full value from the higher full value, then round the difference.
mistakes: Write the currency after every value. The number alone cannot tell you which direction the calculation went.
Turning around in the quote changes the operation. Test it using the two amounts printed in the quote.
The fee is an amount of money with a unit. Subtract it from an amount in that same currency.

examples.title: Exchange pounds for euros
examples.question: At a counter, £1 buys €1.30. An organiser changes £265 into euros. How many euros does the organiser receive?
examples.solution:
For every pound the organiser receives €1.30. Multiply the pounds by \(1.3\).

\(265\times 1.3\) gives €344.50.

examples.title: Exchange euros for pounds
examples.question: A collector has €414. Use the exchange rate £1 = €1.47. Calculate the value in pounds to the nearest penny.
examples.solution:
One pound uses €1.47. Divide the euros by euros per pound.

The calculation is \(414\div 1.47\). Round that result to get £281.63.

examples.title: Deduct the fee before exchanging
examples.question: A customer hands over £277 to buy euros. The bureau first keeps a fee of £3.06. It converts the remaining pounds at £1 = €1.11. How many euros does the customer receive to the nearest cent?
examples.solution:
Take the fee from the pounds. That leaves £273.94 for the exchange.

Multiply this by \(1.11\) euros per pound. The customer receives €304.07 after rounding.

lessons.title: Work with simple interest
lessons.summary: Use the starting deposit and an annual rate to work out simple interest, the ending balance or a missing deposit.
lessons.objective: Use the starting deposit and an annual rate to work out simple interest, the ending balance or a missing deposit.
lessons.before: Write a percentage as a decimal before using the interest formulas.
lessons.ideas:
Work out one year's interest first. A 3.6% rate means 3.6 out of every 100 pounds of the starting deposit per year.

For an annual rate, the time in years is \(\dfrac{\text{months}}{12}\). For instance, 18 months is \(\frac{18}{12}=1.5\) years.

Over the full term, the interest is \(rt\) times the starting deposit. Use \(P=\dfrac{I}{rt}\) if the question gives the interest itself.
lessons.method:
Why is the interest the same each year?

For principal \(P\), annual rate \(r\) written as a decimal and time \(t\) in years, interest is \(I=Prt\). Add the principal only if asked for the balance.

How do I use a term given in months?

Multiply one year's interest by the fraction or decimal number of years. Keep the full values until the final answer.

How can I recover the starting deposit?

Multiply your proposed deposit by the annual decimal rate and the number of years. You should recover the stated interest.
mistakes: A balance and interest earned answer different questions. Use the wording of the final line to decide which to give.
Do not put 18 in the years box for 18 months. Convert it to years first.
Dividing by the one-year rate ignores how long the money was there. Use the complete term.

examples.title: Calculate simple interest earned
examples.question: A school association saves £3920 at \(5\)% simple interest per year. Find the interest it earns in 6 years to the nearest penny.
examples.solution:
Interest for one year is \(5\)% of £3920, which is \(196\) pounds. Keep this value for the next step.

Multiply that same annual amount by 6. The interest is £1176.00.

examples.title: Allow for months in a simple-interest term
examples.question: A school club deposits £4345 for 21 months. It earns \(6.7\)% simple interest per year, proportionally for a part of a year. Find the interest earned to the nearest penny.
examples.solution:
The time in years is \(\frac{21}{12}\). The rate is quoted per year.

Multiply the full annual interest of \(291.115\) pounds by \(\frac{21}{12}\). The interest is £509.45.

examples.title: Find the principal from the interest earned
examples.question: A repair fund earned £4875.00 of simple interest over 5 years at 5% per year. Find the original amount in the fund.
examples.solution:
Over 5 years the interest is \(\frac{5}{100}\times 5\), or 25%, of the starting amount.

Divide the interest by \(0.25\). The original amount was £19500.00.

lessons.title: Work with annual compound interest
lessons.summary: Apply a fixed annual multiplier, separate interest from balance and compare simple and compound accounts.
lessons.objective: Apply a fixed annual multiplier, separate interest from balance and compare simple and compound accounts.
lessons.before: Write a percentage as a decimal before using the interest formulas.
lessons.ideas:
At a fixed annual rate \(r\) written as a decimal, each year multiplies the current balance by \(1+r\). For a 4.2% rate the factor is \(1.042\).

For principal \(P\) and \(n\) full years, the balance is \(P(1+r)^n\). To find interest only, take the original amount from the ending balance.

Use the starting balance for every simple-interest calculation and the changing balance for the compound account. Use each account's own rate.
lessons.method:
What changes when interest is compounded?

At 4%, a £650 deposit earns £26.00 in year one and grows to £676.00. The second year starts with £676.00 and earns £27.04.

How do I find the balance or just the interest?

Enter the multiplier in brackets with the exponent. Keep the full balance for the subtraction and round the amount requested at the end.

How do I compare two offers fairly?

Work out both balances before choosing the higher one. Subtract using the full values if the question asks for a difference.
mistakes: The multiplier needs the original 100% plus the added percentage. The rate alone gives one year's interest, not the updated balance.
The exponent is the number of annual updates. Multiplying the rate by the years gives a simple-interest calculation.
A compound account can finish lower if its rate is lower. Use the numbers given before deciding.

examples.title: Find a balance with annual compounding
examples.question: A library fund saves £5595 at \(5.8\)% interest, compounded annually. Calculate its balance after 3 full years to the nearest penny.
examples.solution:
Each year the current balance is multiplied by \(1.058\).

Apply that multiplier 3 times. The calculation \(5595\times 1.058^{3}\) gives £6626.09 to the nearest penny.

examples.title: Find just the interest from an annual balance
examples.question: A tool library puts £6020 into an account paying \(7.5\)% compound interest per year. How much interest is earned in 5 full years? Give the answer to the nearest penny.
examples.solution:
The annual multiplier is \(1.075\). Multiply the deposit by this multiplier raised to the power 5.

The balance rounds to £8642.49. Subtract the original deposit from the full balance and round the interest to £2622.49.

examples.title: Compare simple and compound interest
examples.question: Two accounts each start with £6445 and both pay \(3.3\)% per year. One pays simple interest. The other compounds annually. How much higher is the compound balance after 2 full years? Give the difference to the nearest penny.
examples.solution:
For simple interest add the same yearly amount to the starting balance. The simple balance rounds to £6870.37.

For compound interest use the annual multiplier \(1.033\) with exponent 2. The compound balance rounds to £6877.39.

Subtract the simple balance from the full compound balance, then round. The difference is £7.02.
